options.B: The activity requires investigation because payment parties, routing and instruction changes can be material trade-related red flags even when total value matches forecast.
options.C: Prioritize the third-party payment analysis because it directly changes the funds flow; treat route and instruction changes as supporting context rather than separate escalation triggers.
options.D: The customer should be re-profiled to include third-party payments and complex routes as normal activity if the pattern has persisted for most of the year.

questions.why: Forecast consistency is not just a total-value test. The changed transaction structure can indicate trade-based financial-crime risk and must be understood before the profile is rewritten.
questions.weaker: A overweights aggregate volume. C fragments related red flags. D normalizes unexplained behavior instead of validating it.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — TBFC red flags and ongoing activity review; competency 4.4

questions.stem: During a periodic review, the analyst sees that a customer's prior transaction-monitoring alerts were repeatedly closed as “known customer” without analysis. The current KYC profile still describes activity from four years ago. Recent transactions include new countries and higher-value transfers. What is the most appropriate review response?

options.A: Rely on the prior alert closures unless internal audit has formally challenged them, because KYC should not second-guess completed monitoring decisions.
options.B: Update the profile to reflect the recent countries and values, then close the review because the change has been documented.
options.C: Reassess actual activity against a refreshed business profile, test whether earlier alert rationales were adequate, and escalate unresolved customer-risk or control concerns appropriately.
options.D: Treat the weak alert notes as evidence of employee misconduct and refer the monitoring analysts for disciplinary action before continuing KYC review.

questions.why: The stale profile and unexplained alert closures create both customer-risk and control-quality questions. The analyst should rebuild the expected-activity baseline, review the material activity, and escalate unresolved concerns rather than simply carrying forward old conclusions.
questions.weaker: A assumes prior closure equals quality. B documents the new behavior without understanding it. D jumps to a personnel conclusion outside the evidence and does not resolve the customer risk.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — periodic review, TM linkage and control effectiveness; competency 4.4

questions.stem: A global bank centralizes KYC review in another country. A local analyst wants to send passport copies, tax records and adverse-media notes to the offshore review team through the bank's approved case-management platform. Local privacy law restricts cross-border transfers unless specified safeguards are met. The review team has a legitimate business need. What is the best response?

options.A: Send the records through the approved internal platform because the offshore team has a legitimate KYC need and the bank already controls access, encryption and retention inside that environment.
options.B: Hold all cross-border transfer until local privacy or legal confirms that the offshore review arrangement is permitted, then send the complete case file so both teams work from identical evidence.
options.C: Transfer only identity and risk-summary data now under data minimization, and send tax records or adverse-media source documents later only if the offshore reviewer specifically requests them.
options.D: Confirm the required legal and policy safeguards first; if transfer is permitted, minimize the data, restrict access and use the authorized platform.

questions.why: Need-to-know and secure systems are necessary but may not be sufficient where law imposes cross-border-transfer conditions. The correct response combines legal basis/safeguards, minimum necessary data, and authorized handling.
questions.weaker: A treats platform security and business need as substitutes for transfer-law safeguards. B correctly pauses for permission but assumes the full file should then be sent rather than minimizing data. C applies minimization but assumes transfer authority before confirming the legal/policy basis. D addresses permission, minimization, access and approved transmission in the right order.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — data security/privacy and cross-border restrictions; competency 5.1

questions.stem: An internal quality review finds that a customer's date of birth was entered incorrectly three years ago. The wrong date was used in repeated sanctions and PEP screening and in risk scoring. The correct date is supported by reliable documents. Which remediation is most defensible?

options.A: Correct the master data through the controlled process and rerun current screening/risk scoring; preserve prior decisions because they were made from the data available to analysts at the time.
options.B: Correct the data through the controlled process, preserve the audit history, assess which prior screening and risk decisions could have been affected, and rerun or remediate those controls where the error could have changed an outcome.
options.C: Correct the date and reconstruct screening and risk decisions across the full three-year period before closing the remediation, even if an initial impact assessment suggests some reviews could not have been affected.
options.D: Correct the master profile prospectively and perform a targeted quality review of recent screening alerts; older decisions can remain unless a regulator or audit function requests reconstruction.

questions.why: Data quality is a control dependency. The remediation must address both the source record and downstream decisions that relied on it, while preserving traceability of the correction.
questions.weaker: A fixes the present but does not assess whether the known data error impaired prior controls. C may be disproportionate by reopening everything without first assessing material impact. D arbitrarily limits remediation to recent cases rather than the decisions that could actually have been affected.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — data quality, screening and audit trail; competency 5.1/5.3

questions.stem: A KYC investigator is reviewing a complex customer and wants to copy documents to a local desktop folder and a personal encrypted USB drive so they can work while traveling. Both devices use strong encryption, and the investigator plans to delete the copies after the review. Which response best reflects KYC data-governance principles?

options.A: Allow the copies because encryption and planned deletion reduce the confidentiality risk to an acceptable level.
options.B: Allow the desktop folder but not the USB drive, because local fixed storage is less likely to be lost.
options.C: Use storage and transfer methods authorized by data-classification, access, retention and security policy; encryption does not itself authorize a prohibited copy.
options.D: Permit the USB drive if a second employee records the files copied, because dual control addresses the main risk.

questions.why: Security controls such as encryption do not replace authorization, retention rules, or institutional data-handling policy. KYC data should remain in approved systems and be shared/stored only by permitted methods.
questions.weaker: A and B assume technical security equals authorization. D misuses dual control as a substitute for data-governance requirements.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — data security/privacy and approved storage; competency 5.1

questions.stem: An analyst must summarize a high-risk customer's adverse-media issue. The evidence is: a reputable newspaper alleges bribery based on unnamed sources; the customer denies the allegation; no charge or regulator action is found; the customer's government-contracting business and PEP association are verified. Which profile wording is strongest?

options.A: “Reputable media alleges bribery from unnamed sources. No official action found as of review date; customer denies it. Verified government-contracting and PEP links increase relevance; allegation remains uncorroborated and is escalated for EDD.”
options.B: “Customer is likely involved in bribery because the reputable-media allegation, PEP association and government-contracting activity reinforce one another; the denial and absence of charges do not outweigh the combined indicators.”
options.C: “No substantiated bribery was identified because there is no official action; record the article as unverified background and maintain existing controls unless new evidence emerges.”
options.D: “Customer denies the article and no official action was found. Note the PEP and government-contracting links, retain the current high-risk rating, and revisit at periodic review.”

questions.why: The strongest note separates allegation, verified facts, absence of official corroboration, customer response, analyst relevance assessment, and action. It is reproducible without converting an allegation into a fact or dismissing it.
questions.weaker: B is conclusory. C treats absence of enforcement as proof of absence. D is too vague to show what was reviewed or why it matters.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — Present/customer profile and adverse-media documentation; competency 5.2

questions.stem: A customer profile will be used by transaction monitoring, periodic-review analysts, sanctions teams, internal audit and senior approvers. Which information architecture makes the profile most useful across those audiences?

options.A: Record purpose/expected activity, verified identity/ownership, key risks/mitigants, material discrepancies, source references, decisions/approvals, and unresolved items affecting monitoring or review.
options.B: Use a detailed chronology of the material research steps and evidence so downstream teams can reconstruct the case without relying heavily on analyst summary judgments.
options.C: Keep the profile concise: final risk rating, purpose, products, expected activity, and unresolved items; link to the evidence file rather than restating ownership and adverse-media details.
options.D: A business-friendly summary written primarily to justify the relationship, with technical compliance details kept out of the main profile to reduce complexity.

questions.why: A customer profile is a control artifact, not just a narrative. It should let multiple downstream users understand who the customer is, what activity is expected, what risks were found, how they were resolved, and what remains open, with enough source traceability to verify the analysis.
questions.weaker: B is exhaustive rather than decision-useful. C omits the evidence and assumptions downstream controls rely on. D biases the document toward advocacy instead of objective risk communication.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — who reads the customer profile / Present step; competency 5.2

questions.stem: A negative-news alert comes from an article in a language none of the local analysts speak. A machine translation says the customer “was convicted,” but a bilingual employee informally reads the original and says it actually states the customer “testified in a conviction case” involving someone else. How should the profile record the issue?

options.A: Record “negative media false positive” based on the bilingual employee's interpretation and remove the translated alert from the file.
options.B: Record the machine-translated allegation because automated translation provides a consistent evidentiary standard across customers.
options.C: Record the initial translation issue, the identity/context ambiguity, the reliable language validation used to resolve it, and the rationale for the final classification.
options.D: Document the final validated classification and supporting source; omit the machine-translation error from the profile if it did not affect the final decision.

questions.why: Good profile writing preserves how the issue arose and how it was resolved. The note should distinguish the automated interpretation from the validated context, show the source of resolution, and support future reviewers if the alert reappears.
questions.weaker: A may rely on an informal opinion without adequate documentation. B treats an error-prone tool as authoritative. D loses useful audit context and may cause repeated rework.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — source validation/translation false positives and profile documentation; competency 5.2/5.3

questions.stem: A relationship manager collects all KYC documents for a high-value customer, verifies the copies against originals, performs the risk assessment, approves the customer and loads the expected-activity parameters into the system. A later review finds the file factually accurate. What is the strongest control concern?

options.A: Treat the concentration of duties as a process observation rather than a material control issue because the later quality review confirmed that the KYC facts, screening and risk outcome were accurate.
options.B: The relationship manager should not have loaded the expected-activity parameters, but the collection, verification and approval steps can remain with one person.
options.C: Treat the commercial conflict as the main issue; a separate senior approval can compensate for limited operational segregation if the file itself is complete and accurate.
options.D: The process lacks appropriate segregation/dual control: independent checking and approval reduce error and collusion risk even when the resulting file later proves accurate.

questions.why: Dual controls are preventive. Their value is not disproved by an accurate file. Combining collection, verification, risk decision and system setup in one person removes independent challenge and increases collusion/error risk.
questions.weaker: A evaluates the control only by outcome. B addresses one system step but not the broader concentration of duties. C mistakes seniority for independence.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — dual controls/four-eyes and segregation of duties; competency 5.3

questions.stem: An analyst overrides a model-generated medium-risk rating to high because reliable external evidence shows opaque control arrangements the model does not capture. The override is approved. Which record best supports a defensible audit trail?

options.A: The final high-risk rating and approver name, because the underlying model score is superseded once the override is authorized.
options.B: The original model output, the material evidence that prompted the override, the analyst's rationale, date, approver/authority, resulting control requirements, and any related model-governance issue.
options.C: Retain the complete KYC evidence set and a note that analyst judgment was applied; detailed override logic can remain in the approver workflow if the final rating and approval are visible in the customer record.
options.D: The analyst's email to the approver, provided the email thread shows agreement and the customer was ultimately categorized as high risk.

questions.why: A good audit trail allows a future reviewer to reconstruct both the system result and why it was overridden, who had authority, and what consequences followed. It should also preserve the control/methodology issue if relevant.
questions.weaker: A erases the original decision path. C is voluminous but not explanatory. D may be supporting evidence but is not a complete controlled record of the decision.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — risk overrides, Present step and auditability; competency 5.3

questions.stem: A sanctions alert was cleared two years ago as a false positive. A new list update adds an alias that makes the alert appear stronger, and the case is reopened. Which prior documentation would most help the new reviewer reassess the case efficiently and defensibly?

options.A: The prior false-positive conclusion, the analyst/reviewer names, and the customer identity documents used at the time, because the new reviewer can repeat the comparison against the updated list.
options.B: The identifiers compared and the final clearance rationale, plus the customer’s then-current identity document; detailed list-version and alias history can be reconstructed from the screening platform if needed.
options.C: The prior screening score, threshold, customer identity fields and clearance date, because those show that the alert met the institution’s technical standard for false-positive closure at the time.
options.D: The identifiers compared, source/list version or date, material matching and conflicting facts, clearance rationale, reviewer/approval details, and any known alias or transliteration considerations.

questions.why: A reusable screening decision requires more than a conclusion. It should show what evidence supported the clearance so the new reviewer can determine whether the new alias changes the prior reasoning.
questions.weaker: A supports reconstruction but loses the actual reasoning and source context. B is stronger but assumes historical system data will remain available and omits potentially material alias/list context. C records model mechanics without enough human match analysis. D gives the next reviewer the evidence trail needed to understand what changed.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — documenting false positives/name screening; competency 5.3/2.3

questions.stem: A low-risk customer is not due for periodic review for another 18 months. The customer is appointed to a prominent public function and becomes a PEP under the institution's policy. No unusual transactions are observed. What is the best KYC response?

options.A: Wait until the scheduled review because the absence of unusual transactions means the risk change has not affected account behavior.
options.B: Trigger an event-driven review now to update PEP status, risk rating, source-of-wealth/funds and approval/monitoring requirements as applicable.
options.C: Update the PEP flag and screening/monitoring controls immediately, while deferring the broader profile refresh to the next scheduled review if wealth and activity remain unchanged.
options.D: Increase transaction-monitoring sensitivity but leave the KYC profile unchanged until the customer conducts a transaction related to the public role.

questions.why: A material change in public function changes customer risk independent of transaction behavior. Event-driven KYC should update the facts and controls that depend on that risk before the next scheduled review.
questions.weaker: A delays a known change. C separates a key risk flag from the profile and controls it should affect. D changes downstream monitoring without updating the underlying KYC basis.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — ongoing due diligence/PEP status change; competency 5.4

questions.stem: A corporate customer moves its headquarters to a higher-risk jurisdiction and restructures ownership. No new natural person crosses the institution's formal 25% ownership threshold, but voting agreements now give two minority investors joint power to appoint most directors. The customer is not due for review for a year. Which action is strongest?

options.A: No event-driven review is needed because no new shareholder crossed the formal ownership percentage threshold.
options.B: Update geographic risk and monitoring now; reassess control/UBO at the next scheduled review because no natural person's ownership percentage crossed the policy threshold.
options.C: Wait for the scheduled review but increase screening frequency in the meantime because both changes are already documented.
options.D: Trigger a targeted review of geography, ownership/control, UBO determination and risk rating because the jurisdiction and control structure materially changed even without a threshold-crossing shareholder.

questions.why: Event-driven review is driven by material change, not only a numerical ownership threshold. New geography and control rights can alter risk and beneficial-control analysis immediately.
questions.weaker: A and B ignore control through other means. C delays reassessment of known material changes and treats screening frequency as a substitute for KYC refresh.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — ongoing review, ownership/control and geographic change; competency 5.4

questions.stem: An existing medium-risk customer is the subject of an internal suspicious-activity escalation after a significant behavior change. The MLRO files a report where required. The customer's ownership and identification data are unchanged. Which KYC maintenance action is most defensible?

options.A: Treat the behavior change and reporting event as triggers to reassess the customer profile, expected activity, risk rating and EDD/monitoring needs, while preserving reporting confidentiality.
options.B: Leave KYC unchanged because suspicious-activity reporting belongs to the MLRO and does not alter customer identity or ownership.
options.C: Move the customer to high risk with enhanced monitoring now because the internal suspicion threshold was met and a report was filed, then reconsider the rating at the next scheduled review.
options.D: Wait until the next periodic review so the KYC team does not risk learning confidential details about the suspicious-activity process.

questions.why: KYC and monitoring are linked. A material behavior change—and in many programs a suspicious-activity filing—can trigger refresh even when static identity fields are unchanged. The profile should be reassessed without disclosing or mishandling confidential reporting information.
questions.weaker: B artificially separates controls that depend on the same behavior. C treats a report as proof and fixes the rating without reassessment. D preserves a stale profile despite a known trigger.
questions.source: ACAMS Study Guide v1.2 — transaction monitoring, SAR-triggered refresh and ongoing due diligence; competency 5.4
